title: "What I Learned from the GMDS Biostatistics Competition 2026"
subtitle: "Ensembling heterogeneous treatment effect estimators, and where the pipeline breaks when every component is evaluated separately"
author: "Imad El Badisy"
date: "2026-08-20"
categories: [R, causal-inference, biostatistics, machine-learning]

---

Participating in the **GMDS Biostatistics Competition 2026** was a useful opportunity to test an idea that I had been interested in for some time: can heterogeneous treatment effect estimation be made more robust by combining several learners rather than relying on a single model?

My submission used a unified R pipeline for the five competition tasks. The central idea was to estimate individual treatment effects using several approaches, including random forests, elastic-net models, gradient boosting, and causal forests[^pkgs], and then combine their subgroup assignments through a co-association consensus framework inspired by Evidence Accumulation Clustering.

The competition was particularly valuable because the evaluation did not simply tell me whether the overall approach worked. It highlighted **which components of the pipeline were robust and which ones need to be redesigned**.

## What worked

One lesson was that combining complementary evidence can be effective for detecting treatment effect heterogeneity.

For this task, I combined three signals: the GRF calibration test, an interaction test between treatment and the estimated subgroup, and a comparison of treatment effects between the subgroup and its complement. The final decision was based on majority voting.

This reinforced my view that heterogeneous treatment effect detection should not necessarily depend on a single diagnostic.

The consensus framework also appeared useful for estimating the overall size of a treatment-responsive subgroup. This suggests that ensemble approaches may capture the **population structure** reasonably well even when individual patient assignments remain imperfect.

## What I would change

The competition also exposed several weaknesses that I would address differently in a future analysis.

### 1. Variable selection needs its own ensemble strategy

I used elastic-net regression with treatment-covariate interactions to distinguish predictive from prognostic variables. Variables with non-zero interaction coefficients were classified as predictive, while non-zero main effects were considered prognostic.

In retrospect, this was probably too dependent on a single model.

Using `lambda.min` is primarily designed to optimize predictive performance rather than recover the true sparse variable structure. In future work, I would investigate approaches such as:

* stability selection,
* stronger penalization such as `lambda.1se`,
* hierarchical interaction selection,
* model-based variable importance from causal forests,
* and consensus variable selection across several HTE learners.

The same ensemble philosophy used for treatment effect estimation should probably also be applied to variable discovery.

### 2. Do not binarize CATE estimates too early

For subgroup assignment, each learner's CATE estimate was converted into a binary benefiter/non-benefiter decision according to whether the estimated treatment effect was above or below zero. These binary partitions were then combined through a co-association matrix.

This is simple and robust, but it discards a large amount of information.

A predicted treatment effect of `0.001` and another of `1.5` receive exactly the same label, while two estimates close to zero but with opposite signs are considered completely different.

In a future implementation, I would preserve the continuous CATE predictions longer and build the consensus directly from standardized treatment-effect estimates.

For example, instead of clustering binary assignments, one could cluster patients using the matrix

$$
\left[
\hat{\tau}_{RF},\;
\hat{\tau}_{glmnet},\;
\hat{\tau}_{XGB},\;
\hat{\tau}_{GRF}
\right].
$$

This would allow both the direction and magnitude of predicted treatment benefit to contribute to the consensus.

### 3. Subgroup discovery and treatment-effect estimation must be separated

This is probably the most important lesson.

After identifying the subgroup, I estimated treatment effects within the subgroup and its complement using AIPW through `grf::average_treatment_effect()`.

However, the same dataset contributed to both subgroup discovery and subsequent estimation.

That creates an important statistical problem: we identify patients partly because they appear to have large treatment effects and then estimate the treatment effect in those same selected patients.

Even a sophisticated estimator such as AIPW does not automatically remove the bias introduced by **data-adaptive subgroup selection**.

In future work, I would therefore use a fully cross-fitted pipeline:

$$
\text{training data} \rightarrow \text{CATE model} \rightarrow \text{subgroup rule}
$$

followed by application of that rule to independent out-of-fold observations:

$$
\text{out-of-fold patients} \rightarrow \text{subgroup assignment} \rightarrow \text{treatment-effect estimation}.
$$

Repeated cross-fitting could then be used to stabilize both subgroup membership and effect estimates.

## The broader lesson

The most useful lesson from this competition is that **good subgroup discovery does not automatically imply good treatment-effect estimation**.

There are several distinct statistical problems hidden inside what we often call heterogeneous treatment effect analysis:

$$
\text{Detect HTE} \neq \text{Identify modifiers} \neq \text{Assign patients} \neq \text{Estimate subgroup prevalence} \neq \text{Estimate subgroup treatment effects}.
$$

A method can perform well on one of these objectives and poorly on another.

For future HTE work, I would therefore design the pipeline around these objectives separately, while maintaining a coherent overall framework:

$$
\boxed{
\text{Ensemble CATE estimation} +
\text{Consensus variable selection} +
\text{Continuous consensus subgrouping} +
\text{Cross-fitting} +
\text{Independent effect estimation}
}
$$

That is probably the main value of participating in methodological competitions: not simply trying to rank well, but discovering **where an apparently reasonable statistical pipeline breaks when every component is evaluated separately**.

I will certainly take these lessons into the next version of the approach.

[^pkgs]: The pipeline was built in R using [grf](https://grf-labs.github.io/grf/) for causal forests, the GRF calibration test, and AIPW average treatment effect estimation; [glmnet](https://glmnet.stanford.edu/) for elastic-net variable selection; and [xgboost](https://xgboost.readthedocs.io/) for gradient-boosted CATE estimation. The co-association consensus step was inspired by Evidence Accumulation Clustering (Fred & Jain, 2005, *IEEE TPAMI*).
